# Do field-dependent individuals tend to have lower creativity than field-independent ones? The role of informational cues in electronic brainstorming

Chun Li<sup>a,b,c</sup>†, Xiaolin Mu<sup>a,d</sup>†, Yuanyuan Tan<sup>a,b,c</sup>, Chuanhua Gu a,b,c, Bi Ying Hu<sup>e</sup> and Cuiying Fan<sup>a,b,c</sup>

<sup>a</sup>School of Psychology, Central China Normal University, Wuhan, People’s Republic of China; <sup>b</sup>Key Laboratory of Adolescent Cyberpsychology and Behavior, Ministry of Education, Wuhan, People’s Republic of China; <sup>c</sup>Collaborative Innovation Center of Assessment for Basic Education Quality, Wuhan, People’s Republic of China; <sup>d</sup>Department of Student Affair, Guangzhou Information Engineering Vocational School, Guangzhou, People’s Republic of China; <sup>e</sup>Faculty of Education, University of Macau, Macau, People’s Republic of China

## ABSTRACT

Much research on brainstorming has found that the power of a team can stimulate individual creativity, and that this influence is more prominent in computer-mediated online interactions. However, creativity appears to depend on the outcome of combining certain environmental factors with certain kinds of Individual characteristics. Two experiments using electronic brainstorming were conducted in this study to examine the creative performance of individuals with different cognitive styles in several creative fields and with various environmental cues. Overall, it was found that cognitive styles significantly affected the creativity of individuals. Creative performances of individuals with field-independent cognitive styles were more stable than those of individuals with fielddependent cognitive styles. However, the appearance of environmental cues reversed this particular effect. When cues were present, there were no significant differences between the creativity of fielddependent and field-independent individuals. The findings provide empirical evidence for improving the creativity of field-dependent individuals and have significant implications for education and talent cultivation.

ARTICLE HISTORY Received 15 February 2020 Accepted 7 September 2020

KEYWORDS Cognitive style; creative fields; environmental cues; creativity; electronic brainstorming

Creativity can be defined, from a product perspective (Kaufman & Sternberg, 2010; Sternberg & Lubart, 1991), as the production of novel, surprising, and eye-catching ideas or products (Sternberg, 2017). There are a variety of tools to measure creativity. In addition to traditional paper-and-pencil tests, many studies on creativity have used brainstorming – in which a group of people generate new ideas around a particular area of interest (Osborn, 1957). Advances in information technology have facilitated the development of electronic brainstorming (EBS), a variation of traditional brainstorming that is increasingly used in research on team creativity (Levine et al., 2017). To further develop this method, it is necessary to explore whether particular types of groups are more effective in stimulating creativity.

One type of group is a nominal group, in which group members do not interact during brainstorming, but propose their ideas separately and eventually integrate them into the group results (Taylor et al., 1958). In contrast, interactive groups work together during brainstorming. EBS is the most common type of interactive group, as it combines the advantages of traditional brainstorming and nominal group techniques (Gallupe et al., 1992). In an EBS group, members share their ideas via computer screens, which can generate synergies among group members. In other words, listening to other members’ ideas can activate related concepts in the mind of the listener, which, in turn, can stimulate the listener to generate more novel and creative ideas (Osborn, 1957).

EBS allows parallel input and takes place in real time; it is also convenient and can improve the efficiency of group idea generation (Dennis & Reinicke, 2004). In addition, the anonymity in EBS can reduce the negative consequences of evaluation apprehension (Jessup et al., 1990). Similar to paper-and-pencil tests, EBS experiments evaluate three aspects of the creativity of participants’ ideas: fluency (number of non-redundant ideas) (Kerr & Murthy, 2004), novelty (innovation quality of ideas; Barki & Pinsonneault, 2001), and flexibility (variety of ideas; Baruah & Paulus, 2011; Deuja et al., 2014).

Studies have shown that, under certain conditions, EBS groups perform better than nominal groups in the generation of creative ideas and are superior to traditional brainstorming groups that share ideas face-to-face. However, DeRosa et al. (2007) found that nominal teams generate more non-redundant ideas when the teams are small, while EBS groups perform better when the teams are large.

## Domain generality and specificity of creativity

The domain specificity or domain generality of creativity is a key topic in research on creativity (Julmi & Scherm, 2015; Qian & Plucker, 2018). Some researchers believe that creativity is a general process, as creative activities in different fields require the same components of creativity (Tu & Fan, 2015). Most studies of creativity assume the generality of creativity; although, some have shown that creativity is domain-specific. Environmental factors, such as life experiences related to education and culture, can predict creativity in specific domains (Hong & Milgram, 2010); while many individual factors, such as individual motivations, drive people in different domains to work in their own areas of expertise (Harrington & Chin-Newman, 2017).

Scientific and artistic creativity have received much attention and are often used in comparative studies of domain-specific creativity (Agnoli et al., 2016). In recent years, researchers have explored social creativity and noticed the difference between creativity in dealing with various social issues (such as interpersonal relationships) in daily life and scientific and artistic creativity (Gu et al., 2018).

The Amusement Park Theoretical Model of Creativity integrates the domain specificity and generality of creativity (Kaufman & Baer, 2004). This integration provides researchers with a new perspective, which suggests that factors such as intelligence, personality, and motivations have different effects on creativity across various domains. Domain-general factors, such as divergent and convergent creative thinking modes, have universal explanatory power across various domains (Goldschmidt, 2016), while other factors are specific to certain domains; empathy, for instance, is only significantly related to creativity in social fields (Dostál et al., 2017).

Research in this area has examined what factors have general effects and what factors have domain-specific effects on creativity. This study focused on the stable characteristics of individuals’ cognitive styles to explore how they influence creativity across various domains.

## Cognitive style and creativity

Cognitive style, also known as thinking style, refers to the preference, habitual manner, or tendency that individuals exhibit when organizing, processing, and representing information (Riding &

Rayner, 2013). However, few cognitive styles have been sufficiently confirmed and their universal explanatory power has not been demonstrated.

Field dependence-independence is a cognitive style that is based on rich empirical evidence and has universal explanatory power in human psychology and behavior. The term “field cognitive style” was coined by Witkin and Goodenough (1977) – based on their finding that individuals have different degrees of dependence on the environment. Individuals who are easily affected by environmental factors are field-dependent and can better perceive and use information to solve problems in an unstructured environment. Individuals who are not susceptible to environmental factors are fieldindependent; they prefer automated information processing in an unstructured environment, using their existing thinking and action patterns. The Embedded Figures Test (EFT) is a commonly used tool for measuring cognitive style. The original EFT was developed by Witkin et al. (1977). Song et al. (1988) created the Chinese version of the EFT based on the English version, which has been widely used in studies of cognitive styles.

Cognitive processes, especially divergent thinking processes, have long been a major topic in creativity research (Ward & Kennedy, 2017). As an important component of cognition, cognitive style is inevitably involved in the cognitive processes of creative activities and influences creativity. Research has shown that field dependence-independence is a relatively stable and habitual cognitive style that is rarely affected by the environment (Zeng et al., 2010). Walter and Dassonville (2011) found that field-dependent individuals typically recruit a strongly bilateral frontoparietal network when performing the EFT. Research on individual trait creativity using the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking showed that field-independent individuals performed better than did field-dependent individuals on all dimensions of creativity (Miller, 2007). Research on individual creativity using the EFT showed that field-independent and field-dependent individuals only differed in the flexibility of creativity (Hao, 2014). In different domains and emotional states (Kirton, 1976), field cognitive styles have diverse influences on creativity.

The above findings suggest that specific cognitive styles are not necessarily more or less conducive to creativity. The creativity of individuals with different cognitive styles appears to depend on the situation and the type of problem. It is not sufficient to simply measure and compare the creativity of individuals with different cognitive styles. Instead, the interaction effects of cognitive styles and situational factors in specific contexts should be examined. To this end, this study focused on an important environmental factor in EBS experiments – environmental cues.

## Environmental cues and creativity

An environmental cue is any object in participants’ experimental environment that provides a cue to the problem they are trying to solve (Ward, 1969). It is an objectively existing entity in the environment where the participant is present, in the form of contextual cues, pictures, or other objects (Amabile, 1983; Paulus & Dzindolet, 1993). In studies of creativity using EBS, researchers pay more attention to the influence of environmental cues such as “others’ ideas.” Specialized EBS software, such as Group Systems V (Bahli, 2013), is often used to control the ideas presented to participants when studying the influence of ideas on creativity.

Based on the assumption of the chain reaction of ideas, in team brainstorming, exposure to team members’ ideas can activate the conceptual nodes associated with these ideas in the minds of other team members, thus generating ideas that would not appear when working alone (Dugosh et al., 2000). Chain reaction is the foundation of brainstorming as it enables the group to produce more creative ideas. Yagolkovskiy (2016) found that when rare, ordinary, and absurd ideas were presented to participants, rare ideas had a positive influence on creativity as the number of novel ideas that participants put forward increased significantly.

Further evidence comes from Paulus and Brown (2007), who proposed a cognitive-social-motivational model to summarize the research findings on idea generation and creativity in groups, noting the importance of others’ ideas. The model highlights that sharing ideas and noticing others’ ideas during group brainstorming are key factors in improving team creativity. Michinov et al. (2015) noted that most creative activities involved members noticing others’ ideas and using them to promote their own ideas. Paulus subsequently performed extensive research that further supplemented and improved the model (Baruah & Paulus, 2016; Korde & Paulus, 2017; Paulus et al., 2013).

Inspired by the model, other researchers found that, apart from highly novel ideas, the proposal of sensitive ideas can also stimulate creativity. Sensitive ideas are often related to political thoughts or value judgments, which can lead to a wide range of responses and discussions among members, thus promoting creativity (Coursey et al., 2018).

Some researchers disagreed with the conclusion that exposure to others’ ideas during group brainstorming can promote team creativity (e.g. Kohn & Smith, 2011). They argued that paying attention to others’ ideas in the process of idea generation can be harmful to the individual’s thinking process, which is detrimental to the improvement of creativity.

There may be two reasons for the inconsistencies of these research conclusions. First, different individuals benefit to different degrees from the environmental cues provided by others’ ideas. When solving problems, individuals who are easily affected by the environment may benefit from others’ ideas. In contrast, individuals who are not susceptible to the environment are accustomed to solving problems in their own ways and being exposed to others’ ideas may disturb their thinking process. Individuals who are susceptible to the environment tend to have a field-dependent cognitive style, while those who are not susceptible tend to have a field-independent cognitive style. Given the consistent differences in cognitive style between field-dependent and field-independent individuals, it is likely that they will also show differences in creativity during creative activities.

Second, in an EBS task, participants are required to generate as many ideas as possible according to the problem situation, which depends on the research purpose. Some problem situations are related to solving social problems, while others involve solving scientific problems. Different individuals are good at different problem areas, and their creative performance may differ on different tasks.

This study tested the above two inferences through two experiments based on previous studies, in which individuals with different cognitive styles were required to generate creative ideas for dealing with problems in different domains and with different environmental cues. Further, this study examined the influence of task types and environmental cues (others’ ideas) on the creative performance of individuals with different cognitive styles, the research framework is shown in Figure 1. We report all measures, manipulations, exclusions, and the method of determining the sample size. Sensitivity power analysis is shown in Appendix A. The questionnaire of control variables and calculation are shown in Appendix B.

## Preliminary experiment

Before the formal experiments, we conducted a preliminary experiment to collect ideas and built a database of ideas. University students were randomly recruited through posters, a total of 325 (266 female) participants aged between 17 and 25 $( M _ { \mathrm { a g e } } = 2 0 . 0 6 ,   S D = 1 . 8 1 )$ participated in the pre-liminary experiment in exchange for ¥50 (approximately \$7.20). Using a between-groups experimental design, participants were randomly assigned to one of only two conditions: (1) scientific task condition (n = 162), (2) social task condition (n = 163). In accordance with the existing research paradigm, participants were asked to enter and save their ideas onto the Word document within 15 min, based on a scientific or social task (see Experiment 1 “The brainstorming tasks”).

Fifteen participants modified the data type to cause data loss in the scientific task, resulting in 310 data points (252 female; $M_{ age } = 20.08, \; SD = 1.81$ . All data generated by the 163 valid participants – who had participated in the experiments and completed the social tasks – were collected to establish a social task database of ideas; 1,723 non-redundant ideas were included in the social task database. Similarly, the data generated by 147 valid participants – who completed the scientific tasks – were collected to create a scientific task database of ideas; 1,685 non-redundant ideas were included in the scientific task database. Therefore, the results of the preliminary experiment would be used for the grading of Experiments 1 and 2.

## Experiment 1

Previous studies have shown that field-dependent individuals have a higher level of social competence (Yang et al., 2012) and are more likely to recognize and understand the emotions of others than are field-independent individuals (Wo et al., 2004). This capacity for empathy is stronger among social science students than students of other sciences (Kidron et al., 2018), and field-independent individuals are more capable of abstract logical reasoning (Wang & Ou, 2004), which is an essential ability for scientific research, than are field-dependent individuals. Based on the above, we proposed the following hypotheses to explore the influence of task type and cognitive style on creativity.

H1a: Regarding the performance of integrated social and scientific tasks, individuals with field-independent cog nitive styles are more creative than are those with field-dependent cognitive styles.

H1b: Field-dependent individuals are more creative in social tasks, while field-independent individuals are more creative in scientific tasks.

## Method

## Participants and design

Forty participants (33 female) aged 17–24 years $( M _ { \mathrm { a g e } } = 2 0 . 2 0 , \; 5 D = 1 . 6 0 )$ participated in Experiment 1 for ¥50. During the screening process, 64 university students were randomly recruited and tested using a revised Chinese version of the EFT. With reference to Wang and Zhou (2006), we ranked the participants from low to high EFT scores, and selected the top 30% and bottom 30% of participants to participate in the experiment. Thus, participants were sorted into two groups based on their EFT scores: the 20 participants with scores in the top 30% (≤ 13.50 points) were classified into the typical field-dependent group, and the 20 participants with scores in the bottom 30% (≥ 17.50 points) were classified into the typical field-independent group. The 24 participants (13.50–17.50 points) who were not selected did not participate in the follow-up experiment.

## Apparatus and stimuli

Measures of cognitive style. The EFT was used to test participants’ cognitive styles. The test required participants to locate and outline a simple figure embedded within complex figure using a pen. It consisted of three parts each lasting four minutes: the first part contained nine questions and the second and third parts each contained 10 questions. The first part was for practice only and was not graded; however, it was used to check whether the participants understood the test requirements. Those who failed to understand the requirements would be excluded from the following tests. In the second and third parts, 0.5 points were awarded per correct answer on questions 1 and 2, 1 point each on questions 3 and 4, and 1.5 points each on questions 5–10. The total score for the test was 24 points.

The brainstorming tasks. 1. Scientific task: What would the world be like without gravity? The task was selected from the study by Hu and Adey (2002). 2. Social task: How can we make our school (university) better? The task was selected from the studies by Baruah and Paulus (2011) and Deuja et al. (2014).

Apparatus. We installed a Word document on the computers.

## Procedure

Based on the EFT scores of 64 university students, 20 participants in the field-dependent group and 20 in the field-independent group entered the laboratory at the same time. The experiment began after the experimenter introduced the experimental procedure.

Participants were first required to think independently about the brainstorming task shown on the computer screen, produce as many ideas as possible, and enter and save the ideas into the Word document within 15 min. After the first round of the brainstorming task, participants received a 5- minute break and started the second EBS task, which had the same time limit and experimental procedure as the first round. The order of social and scientific tasks was balanced in the order of ABBA: participants either performed the social task first then the scientific task or vice versa. Finally, participants were paid and thanked for their participation.

## Measurement

Two independent raters, both hypothesis and treatment blind, were used. Raters were provided with a detailed coding guide that explained how to identify redundant ideas and to calculate the score of ideas (Bouchard & Hare, 1970).

Fluency was scored as the total number of non-redundant ideas produced by participants, with each idea worth one point. Scoring was based on the method used by Coursey et al. (2018): two raters simultaneously graded 25% of the experimental materials for the social tasks and 25% of the materials for the scientific tasks. The internal consistency between the scores was measured by the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), which was 0.74 for social tasks and 0.97 for scientific tasks, suggesting good internal consistency. Subsequently, one of the raters continued to evaluate the remaining experimental materials for the social tasks, and the other rater continued to evaluate the remaining materials for the scientific tasks. Finally, the fluency scores were calculated using the scores given by the raters for all materials.

Novelty was scored according to the number of times an idea appeared: the lower the frequency of an idea, the higher the novelty score. This study referred to the scoring method in the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking (Torrance, 1966), which calculated novelty based on the frequency of occurrence of an idea in the database. Ideas with a frequency of occurrence of 3% and above scored 0 points, those with a frequency of between 1% and 2.99% scored 1 point, and those with a frequency of 0.99% or lower scored 2 points. The novelty scores of each idea were then summed to obtain the overall novelty score.

Flexibility refers to the variety of ideas. Referring to the tree-based scoring method proposed by Zheng and Li (2003) to evaluate the flexibility of creativity, all ideas in the database were used to establish an idea tree with three parts: the trunk, branches, and twigs. These three parts contained different levels of category information. Based on the results, the idea tree for social tasks consisted of 2 trunks, 5 branches, and 68 twigs (see Open Practice Section). For example, the trunk, branches, and twigs of the idea tree for the idea of “improving water and power outages” corresponded to the environment, campus, and living services, respectively. The idea tree for scientific tasks consisted of 2 trunks, 6 branches, and 31 twigs. For example, the trunk, branches, and twigs of the idea tree for the idea that “everything would float in the air” corresponded to human, individual, and movement, respectively. We compared each idea of each participant with the twigs, and categorized the idea into the corresponding twig, giving it a score of one point. Each twig was counted only once. After that, the ideas included in the same twig were not scored. Finally, the flexibility score was the sum of all scores of the tree.

Similar to the fluency evaluation, two raters simultaneously graded 25% of the experimental materials. The ICC was 0.89 for social tasks and 0.85 for scientific tasks. One of the raters then evaluated the rest of the experimental materials and the flexibility score was calculated based on the scores given by the raters. The answers of high-score participants (Table 1) and low-score participants (Table 2) were shown using scientific tasks as examples.

## Results

In Experiment 1, the field-dependent and field-independent participants’ creative performance in the social and scientific tasks is reported in Table 3. To test the interaction effects of cognitive style and task type on creativity, a 2 (social task, scientific task) × 2 (field-dependence, field-independence) repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed three times using fluency, novelty, and flexibility as the dependent variable, respectively, with cognitive style as the between-participants variable and task type as the within-participants variable.

For fluency, the main effect of cognitive style was significant, as the fluency of creativity of fieldindependent participants was significantly higher than that of field-dependent participants $F ( 1 , 3 8 ) =$ 5.43, p = .025, $\eta _ { p } ^ { 2 }   =   . 1 3$ . The main effect of task type was significant, as fluency of creativity was significantly higher for scientific than for social tasks F(1,38) = 13.84, $p < . 0 0 1$ $\eta _ { p } ^ { 2 }   =   . 2 7$ . The interaction effect between cognitive style and task type was not significant $F(1,38)=0.51$ $p   =   . 4 8 1$ $\eta _ { p } ^ { 2 } = . 0 1$

The main effect of cognitive style on the novelty of creativity was significant: field-independent participants showed significantly greater novelty in their creativity than did field-dependent participants $F(1,38)=4.14,p=.049,\eta_{p}^{2}=.10$ . The main effect of task type was not significant $F ( 1 , 3 8 ) = 0 . 2 0 , p$ $= . 6 5 7 ,$ $\eta _ { p } ^ { 2 } = . 0 1$ . The interaction effect between cognitive style and task type was not significant F (1,38) = 1.96, p = .170, $\eta _ { p } ^ { 2 } = . 0 5$

The main effect of cognitive style on the flexibility of creativity was significant. Field-independent participants showed significantly higher flexibility than did field-dependent participants $F ( 1 , 3 8 ) =$ 5.33, p = .026, $\eta _ { p } ^ { 2 }   =   . 1 2$ . The main effect of task type on the flexibility of creativity was not significant $F(1,38)=3.88,p=.056,\eta_{p}^{2}=.09$ . The interaction effect between cognitive style and task type was not significant F(1,38) = 1.08, p = .307, $\eta _ { p } ^ { 2 } = . 0 3$

According to the results of Experiment 1, the main effects of cognitive style on the fluency, novelty, and flexibility of creativity were significant, while the main effects of task type on the above three dimensions of creativity were not significant. In both the social and scientific tasks, field-independent participants scored significantly higher than field-dependent participants on the fluency, novelty, and flexibility of creativity, thus verifying H1a. The results suggested that field-independent participants showed a higher level of creativity in the open-problem situation presented in the two experiments. Task type and cognitive style had no significant interaction effect on creativity. Both field-dependent and field-independent participants showed the same level of creativity when completing tasks in different domains, and the creativity of field-independent participants was consistently higher than that of field-dependent participants.

## Discussion

The effect of cognitive style on creativity

The results of Experiment 1 are consistent with those of previous studies (Miller, 2007). Field-independent individuals are rarely dependent on the external environment. They process information according to internal standards or references. Field-dependent individuals rely on the external environment and process information according to external references. In consciousness extraction, field-dependent participants had higher scores than did field-independent participants. In the automatic extraction, field-dependent participants had higher scores than did field-dependent participants (Zeng et al., 2010). Therefore, in a situation with insufficient environmental cues, field-independent individuals could extract more relevant knowledge from memory in a short time and showed greater fluency in their creativity than did field-dependent participants.

Field-independent individuals are not easily affected by external information and can more effectively obtain useful information from the environment in the process of solving problems as compared to field-dependent participants (Chang et al., 2016). This tendency toward active learning and information acquisition may allow field-independent individuals to accumulate a large amount of knowledge and experience in their daily lives. Therefore, when encountering problems, they can exercise effective cognitive restructuring skills to summarize previously accumulated knowledge and experience and apply them to the current problem situation, thereby showing greater flexibility.

Other studies have also shown that cognitive style affects flexibility owing to differences in the gray matter volume of the inferior parietal lobe. Field-independent individuals have larger gray matter volume in this area than do field-dependent participants, and thus have excellent local visual processing ability and the ability to distinguish different types of stimuli, which help promote individuals’ level of flexibility (Hao, 2014).

Field-independent individuals are also more willing to take risks (Chang et al., 2016) than are fielddependent participants, and risk propensity is related to higher creativity (Steidle & Werth, 2013). Being adventurous is a common personality trait of highly creative individuals. The risk propensity of field-independent individuals suggests that they may be more willing to try new and diverse options during idea generation and are less likely to hide their ideas because of social rules or secular constraints, thus showing greater novelty in idea generation tasks.

Field-dependent individuals, who are highly dependent on the environment, were unable to effectively extract and utilize their knowledge in Experiment 1, leading to poorer performance in independent idea generation compared with field-independent individuals. Nevertheless, Experiment 1 only examined the open-problem situation for independent idea generation. Although the results are in line with previous research in many respects, it cannot be concluded that the creativity of fielddependent individuals is poorer than that of field-independent individuals. When processing information, field-dependent individuals tend to rely more on external references, and when solving problems, they tend to rely on “field” as compared to field-independent individuals. Additionally, they are more sensitive to nuances in interpersonal communication (Wo et al., 2004), which may cause field-dependent individuals’ creative performance to differ from that of field-independent individuals.

## The effect of task type on creativity

Participants showed significantly higher fluency of creativity in scientific tasks than in social tasks, whereas flexibility and novelty were not affected by task type. The results of Experiment 1 showed that individuals were more fluent; i.e. able to produce more relevant ideas, in the scientific tasks than in the social tasks. “Flexibility” refers to the variety of ideas. As social tasks are closer to everyday life than scientific tasks, individuals may be able to think about the tasks from multiple angles. Solving scientific problems, in contrast, requires scientific knowledge (Bai et al., 2014), and individuals need to have rich knowledge to draw inferences from other cases in scientific tasks. Therefore, it is more difficult to generate ideas flexibly for scientific than for social tasks, resulting in a decrease in individual flexibility. The novelty of creativity was not affected by task type, indicating that people can create similarly novel ideas in both social and scientific fields.

## The effect of cognitive style and task type on creativity

According to Experiment 1, task type and cognitive style had no significant interaction effects on creativity; however, the creativity of field-independent individuals was consistently higher than that of field-dependent individuals. This indicates that cognitive style is a general factor that has a consistent predictive effect on the creativity of individuals’ independent idea generation in both social and scientific domains.

## Experiment 2

Compared with field-dependent individuals, field-independent individuals have better implicit memory that can be accessed quickly and accurately (Zeng et al., 2010), and they are more effective in obtaining useful information from the environment when solving problems (Chang et al., 2016). Field-dependent individuals not only have poorer cognitive restructuring skills, implicit memory, and reasoning abilities than do field-independent individuals, they also tend to have poorer problem-solving ability (Angeli & Valanides, 2004, 2013). However, when environmental cues are present, they are more likely to benefit from them than are field-independent individuals (Evans et al., 2013). Consequently, we proposed the following hypotheses to explore the influence of environmental cues and cognitive style on creativity:

H2a: Regarding performance when integrating information—with and without cues—individuals with field-inde pendent cognitive styles are far more creative than are individuals with field-dependent cognitive styles.

H2b: Field-dependent individuals are more creative in a situation with environmental cues than in a situation without them, whereas field-independent individuals are more creative in a situation without environmental cues than in a situation with such cues.

## Method

## Participants and design

Participants $( n   =   1 0 7 ,$ 92 female; $M _ { \mathrm { a g e } } = 2 0 . 2 3$ years, SD = 1.92) participated in Experiment 2 in exchange for ¥50. Participants were screened, and 170 university students were newly recruited at random. Using the same screening criteria as in Experiment 1, the 53 participants whose EFT scores were in the top $30\% ( \leq 12.00$ points) were included in the field-dependent group; 22 of them were not assigned environmental cues and 31 were assigned cues. The 54 participants with EFT scores in the bottom 30% (≥ 17.00 points) were included in the field-independent group; 29 of them were assigned no environmental cues and 25 were assigned cues. The 63 participants (12.00–17.00 points) who were not selected did not participate in the follow-up experiment.

## Apparatus and stimuli.

Measures of cognitive style. The measures of cognitive style were the same as in Experiment 1.

The brainstorming tasks. As the main effect of task type was not significant in Experiment 1, only the scientific task was used in Experiment 2 (refer to Experiment 1).

Apparatus. Experiment 2 included a nominal group of three people (task group without environmental cues) and an interactive group (task group with environmental cues). We installed a Word document on the computers for the nominal group. We installed Tencent QQ, an online interactive software program, on the computers for the interactive group. Before the experiment, we prepared three new accounts for the participants in the interactive group and linked them to form a chat group. Each participant used one account to interact with the others, where the account name was the participant’s serial number. Each participant had a distinct profile image to differentiate them from other members. Participants could see the full screen of the group chat window on the computer screen. Participants could enter their ideas into the lower part of the window at any time, which then appeared in the upper part of the window once they were sent. The upper part showed the ideas sent by all group members in chronological order, and the participants could view their or others’ ideas at any time (Figure 2).

## Procedure

Based on the EFT scores of 170 university students, the field-dependent group comprised 53 participants (22 completed the task without environmental cues and 31 completed the task with environmental cues) and the field-independent group included 54 participants (29 completed the task without environmental cues and 25 completed the task with environmental cues). Participants entered the laboratory at the same time and sat in front of the computers in groups of three. The experiment started after the experimenter explained the procedure.

In the absence of environmental cues, the participants generated their own ideas and saved them in a Word document, with no access to the ideas of the other two members. In the presence of environmental cues, the participants used Tencent QQ to save and send their own ideas to the group chat, where they could view their own or others’ ideas at any time. The test lasted 15 min. Finally, participants were paid and thanked for their participation.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 2. Screenshot of the online interactive group.

## Measurement

The measurement method was the same as that in Experiment 1. All ideas generated by the participants were collected and organized. The creativity of each participant was graded according to the fluency, novelty, and flexibility of ideas. The ICC for fluency was 0.98. The novelty scores were evaluated based on the scientific task database method established in Experiment 1, and the flexibility scores were evaluated based on the idea tree method in the scientific task established in Experiment 1, where the ICC for flexibility was 0.89.

## Results

The statistical results for the creative performance of field-dependent and field-independent participants under different experimental conditions are shown in Table 4.

To test the interaction effects of cognitive style and task type on creativity, three 2 (field-dependence, field-independence) × 2 (without cues, with cues) ANOVAs were conducted with fluency, novelty, and flexibility as the dependent variables. The results showed that the main effect of cognitive style on fluency was significant: field-independent participants scored significantly higher on fluency than did field-dependent participants $F(1,103)=5.56,\;p=.020,\;\eta_{p}^{2}=.05$ . The main effect of environmental cues was not significant $F(1,103)=0.59,\;p=.444,\;\eta_{p}^{2}=.01$ , and the interaction effect between cognitive style and environmental cues was not significant $F(1,103)=1.72,p=.193,\eta_{p}^{2}=.02.$

The experimental results verified H2a. The findings of Experiment 1 showed that the fluency, novelty, and flexibility of creativity in scientific tasks were rated significantly higher among field-independent than among field-dependent participants, indicating the consistent influence of cognitive style on creativity in the scientific field. In the absence of environmental cues in Experiment 2, the novelty of ideas was higher among field-independent participants; however, in the presence of environmental cues, field-dependent and field-independent participants produced equally novel ideas. These results verified H2b. Compared with field-dependent participants, field-independent participants showed more stable levels of creativity in both the absence and the presence of environmental cues, which again demonstrated that field-independent participants were not susceptible to the environment.

## Discussion

## Demographic characteristics of creativity

In Experiment 2, there were no significant differences in creativity between genders. Previous studies also found no sex differences in creative divergent thinking (Warren et al., 2018). However, some studies of creative problem-solving suggested that women show greater creativity than do men (Barrett et al., 2013; Peterson et al., 2013). Hardy and Gibson (2017) argued that the equivalence problem in measurement may lead to inconsistent results in studies of gender differences in creativity; that is, female and male participants respond differently to measurement methods. Men were more creative when using indicators of creative achievement (Simonton, 1994), while women were more creative when using indicators of creative potential. As the results of gender differences remain at the level of measurement, they cannot reflect whether gender differences in creativity levels truly exist. In research on creativity, different tasks are likely to produce inconsistent results concerning gender differences.

Graduate students showed significantly lower flexibility in scientific tasks than undergraduate students in their second, third, and fourth years; and no differences were found between other years. This finding may be related to the academic life of graduate students. Graduate students are required to conduct in-depth research in their professional fields and may thus be more accustomed to proposing ideas related to their professional fields that they are knowledgeable about. Therefore, their thinking is limited to a few dimensions, which affects their flexibility in thinking to a certain extent. Research has shown that personal knowledge and experience can affect creativity scores (Runco & Acar, 2010).

## The effect of cognitive style and environmental cues on creativity

Concerning group brainstorming, the difference between the presence and absence of environmental cues is actually the difference between a nominal group and an interactive group. In this study, a nominal group and an interactive group were used in Experiment 2 to compare the effects of two situations, with and without environmental cues. The results showed that environmental cues did not have a significant influence on fluency, novelty, or flexibility; although, this may have been because of the small size of the research groups. Previous studies have shown that, in small teams, a nominal team will produce more non-redundant ideas; however, in large teams, an EBS team will perform better in creative idea generation (DeRosa et al., 2007). Other studies have found that individuals who participate in EBS groups of three do not generate more ideas than do those who work independently (Deuja et al., 2014).

The results of Experiment 2 also verified the findings of Experiment 1. Field-independent participants showed significantly higher fluency, novelty, and flexibility in their creativity than did fielddependent participants, indicating the consistent influence of cognitive style on creativity in scientific fields. Participants with both cognitive styles showed different levels of novelty of creativity in the presence and absence of environmental cues. The advantages of field-independent participants were weakened in the presence of cues, and the creativity of field-dependent individuals tended to increase, showing well-matched levels of novelty.

It is possible that the differences in the performance of participants with different cognitive styles were caused by their ways of perceiving, acquiring, and processing environmental information (Lü et al., 2019). In the absence of environmental cues, field-independent participants tend to use internal cues (Miyake et al., 2001) and explore information in memory related to the problem situation, thus showing better creative performance as compared to field-dependent individuals. In the presence of environmental cues, field-dependent individuals are more susceptible to external cues (Miyake et al., 2001) and are more inclined to use the environment as a reference (Lü et al., 2019), which increases the level of novelty in their creativity as compared to field-independent individuals. Thus, the unique finding of Experiment 2 was that cognitive style and environmental cues had interaction effects on some aspects of creativity.

The cognitive restructuring skills, implicit memory, and reasoning ability of field-dependent individuals are not as good as those of field-independent individuals, and they tend to have poorer problem-solving abilities (Angeli & Valanides, 2004, 2013). However, this does not mean that fielddependent individuals cannot achieve the same level of creativity as field-independent individuals. Field-dependent individuals rely more on the “field” at work to provide visual information related to the current problem scenario and are more likely to benefit from the environment than are field-independent individuals (Evans et al., 2013). This is consistent with our experimental finding that providing environmental cues improves the creativity of field-dependent individuals without affecting the level of creativity of field-independent individuals.

## General discussion

The purpose of the two experiments in this study is to determine the mechanism of the creative field and environmental cues in EBS on the idea-generation of individuals with different cognitive styles. More specifically, this research is to answer the following questions: how does cognitive style affect an individual’s creative idea-generation in EBS? Do these influences depend on the creative fields and environmental cues they are exposed to?

Past research generally believes that field-independent individuals have better perception, acquisition, and processing of environmental information (Chang et al., 2016; Miller, 2007; Steidle & Werth, 2013; Zeng et al., 2010). These individuals have a higher level of cognitive differentiation, systematic reasoning, and cognitive reorganization. They are also more willing to try new ideas and rely less on the environment. These advantages enable field-independent individuals to better extract implicit knowledge under insufficient cues, and to show better fluency, flexibility, and novelty in creative activities. The results of this study are consistent with the results of previous studies. Specifically, Experiment 1 found that field-independent individuals always outperformed field-dependent individuals in generating ideas in social and scientific tasks. Field-independent individuals had higher levels of creativity than did field-dependent individuals, indicating that cognitive style is a general factor in tasks requiring the independent generation of open ideas, and has the same impact on creativity in social and scientific domains. Field-independent individuals make better use of their own knowledge and can quickly analyze problems in a vague problem situation and then search for relevant knowledge in memory as compared to field-dependent individuals. They can present more original ideas in a short time and analyze problems from different angles. Moreover, they are not limited to a few types of problem-solving methods and show higher fluency, novelty, and flexibility in idea generation. However, as field-dependent individuals cannot effectively extract existing knowledge from their memory when the problem is unclear and there are few environmental cues, they show lower creativity than do field-independent individuals.

Unlike the previous results, Experiment 2 found that, in the process of generating ideas, if fielddependent individuals could access the ideas generated by others, the novelty of their creativity did not differ from that of field-independent individuals. This result indirectly suggests that the creativity of field-independent individuals is not always higher than that of field-dependent individuals. Even in scientific tasks, giving enough environmental cues to field-dependent individuals can boost their creativity. This finding updates the results of previous studies. As mentioned above, almost all previous studies favored the creativity of field-independent individuals (Miller, 2007; Wang & Zhou, 2006). However, the experimental results of this study showed that the creativity of field-dependent individuals is not always lower than that of field-independent individuals. In an information-sharing group, the level of creativity of field-dependent individuals was the same as that of field-independent individuals. This suggests that measuring the level of creativity of individuals only under independent working conditions is unfair toward field-dependent individuals and is not conducive to interpreting individuals’ true level of creativity. Moreover, it suggests that, to make full use of the creativity of field-dependent individuals, it would be helpful to provide some environmental cues about the problem to be solved, or encourage them to actively acquire and use information; while it is advisable not to interfere too much with the process of idea generation for field-independent individuals.

Although no significant effect of task type on the creativity of individuals with different cognitive styles was found, previous research suggest that field-dependent individuals tend to perform better in creativity in the social field, whereas field-independent individuals may be more creative in scientific fields. This might suggest that domain specificity is less important for field-dependent individuals than previously suggested. Alternatively, it could be the case that the task used was not able to tap into the specific strengths of field-dependent individuals in the social domain. Field-dependent individuals are more sensitive to environmental cues, and this trait may help them in the creative handling of social affairs. Compared with field-dependent individuals, field-independent individuals have higher levels of cognition and differentiation, as well as stronger systemic reasoning skills, and can better extract implicit knowledge (Zeng et al., 2010). These traits may be helpful to them in solving scientific problems in a creative way; however, this assumption needs to be further verified.

## Conclusion and implications

In this study, the creative expression of individuals with two different cognitive styles – in different task areas and cue environments – was discussed. We found that cognitive styles significantly affected individuals’ creativity. Overall, the creative performances of individuals with field-independent cognitive styles were more stable than those of individuals with field-dependent cognitive styles. However, the appearance of environmental cues will reverse this particular situation. When there are cues, there are no significant differences between the creativity of field-dependent individuals and field-independent individuals.

One of the significant contributions of this study is the finding that thinking and working independently stimulated the creativity of field-independent individuals, whereas the atmosphere of teamwork and the provision of environmental cues boosted the creativity of field-dependent individuals. In terms of theoretical implications, given that current idea generation research knows very little about the potential association between cognitive style and creative fields, and cognitive style and environmental cues, this research may provide insights for idea generation research in the field of creativity and empirical evidence to improve the theoretical research of individual creativity.

Regarding practical implications, educators and talent managers can offer targeted support for creative activities by identifying individuals’ cognitive styles. This study confirmed that neither field-dependent nor field-independent individuals are superior in creativity – they merely have different preferences for types of environments. Therefore, field-dependent individuals can be encouraged to work in teams, where they can interact and collaborate with others to stimulate their creativity. For field-independent individuals, too much guidance or too rigid a framework in the creative process will interfere with their thinking processes and work patterns, hindering their creativity. Allowing them to solve problems in a team will also not lead to a substantial improvement in their creativity.

In addition, the essential difference between the nominal group (without cues) and the interactive group (with cues) used in Experiment 2 is whether interaction occurs. Individuals who have access to cues can interact with information by exposure to the ideas of others, and they generate new ideas based on the ideas of others. Additionally, the ideas of others remain available on the screen and can be read repeatedly. The group members can read at any time according to their needs and then output during the experiment. Each group member is not only the receiver of the ideas, but also the processor and sender of the ideas. For independent individuals, whether they interact with environmental cues or not, their performance is stable and outstanding. However, for field-dependent individuals, this interactive environment will have a subversive impact on their creative performance. As mentioned earlier, field-dependent individuals are more dependent on the environment, which means that their benefits from the environment are also higher. Therefore, researchers need to consider the influence of cognitive style in EBS. To increase the reliability of the research, participants should be provided with an information-rich environment to ensure that participants of both cognitive styles have an equal creative environment.

Finally, This study effectively simulated creative situations in real-life environments and in online interactions using the EBS technique, which enhances the environmental validity of research on creativity. Creativity cultivation activities supported by online measures have advantages in practical applications compared with traditional school teaching activities. The Internet offers rich online resources and can overcome the limitations of time and space, and thus has great potential and value in the cultivation of students’ creativity. Especially for field-dependent individuals, online environments can provide a more information-rich working and learning environment and make up for the shortcomings of the inability to be effectively inspired by implicit knowledge.

## Limitations and future directions

This study had some limitations that should be addressed in future research. First, the research data were collected in mainland China with a limited sample size; and the baseline levels of creativity, intelligence, and academic expertise of the selected participants could not be controlled. In addition, the chosen university was a normal university; therefore, there were more female participants. Therefore, subsequent studies should use larger samples and minimize potential gender bias to enhance the applicability of the research findings. Second, creative tasks include divergent and convergent thinking tasks; however, this study only examined divergent thinking. Convergent thinking tasks should be included in future studies. Third, we found that the creativity of field-dependent individuals can be improved by providing environmental cues; however, we did not determine effective ways to improve the creativity of field-independent individuals, which should be explored in future research.

The last and most important point in Experiment 2 is as follows. When field-dependent individuals were able to access the views of others, the novelty of their ideas was no different from that of fieldindependent individuals. One study pointed out that it is unfair for the brainstorming paradigm to attribute unique ideas to specific members because uniqueness stems from the sharing of ideas and the cross-correlation of ideas in the group (Guegan et al., 2017). Therefore, when analyzing the results, the average score of each group can be calculated and compared between the groups. However, the experimental design of this study is not the same as that of Guegan et al. (2017). The participants in each group of Experiment 2 were randomly assigned after controlling the conditions that each group had both field-dependent and field-independent individuals. By design, the size of the group is limited to three participants, and thus, the proportion of the two cognitive styles in each group is different. This is why we cannot compare the novelty of ideas between groups. We plan to focus on this limitation in subsequent research and make improvements in the experimental design.

## Notes on contributors

Chun Li is a PhD student of the School of Psychology at Central China Normal University (CCNU). Her research interests include creativity and online interpersonal interaction.

Xiaolin Mu is a lecturer in the Guangzhou Information Engineering Vocational School. Her research interests include creativity and educational psychology.

Yuanyuan Tan is a master student in the School of Psychology at CCNU. Her research interests include group creativity and interpersonal interaction.

Chuanhua Gu is a professor in the School of Psychology at CCNU. His research interests include creativity and cyberpsychology.

Bi Ying Hu is a professor in the Faculty of Education at University of Macau. Her research interests include early childhood education and child development.

Cuiying Fan is a professor in the School of Psychology at CCNU. Her research interests include educational psychology and cyberpsychology.
